title: Four messages, one where the AI costs the most
intro:
*Five minutes. Commit before you look.*

Four real-shaped uses of AI in leadership communication. Each involves a substantial amount of AI.

**One of them spends far more trust than the other three combined.** Find it.

Don't ask which involves the most AI, or which subject is most sensitive. Ask what the message is claiming, and whether the part that carries the claim was supplied or generated.

artifacts.label: Message A · the restructure announcement
artifacts.body: Three teams are merging; forty people change reporting line. The COO records 25 minutes of unscripted Q&A with the comms lead: what the decision is, why now, what she considered and rejected, what she's worried about. From that recording: a transcript, a written announcement, an FAQ, a manager briefing pack, and nine translations. **Everything published derives from the recording. AI did all of it except the recording.**

artifacts.label: Message B · the finance system migration
artifacts.body: The system is down over a weekend. Comms feeds the change ticket to a model and asks for a plain-language notice with the dates, the cutoff for expense claims, and who to contact. The draft is checked line by line against the ticket, one wrong time is corrected, and it publishes under the IT service desk's name. **Start to finish, about six minutes of human time.**

artifacts.label: Message C · the monthly recognition note
artifacts.body: A director sends personal appreciation notes to eight people each month. This month she exports the completed-project list from the tracker (names and project titles) gives it to a model, and asks for a warm, personalized note to each person referencing their contribution. She reads all eight, changes a word in two of them, and sends them from her own address.

artifacts.label: Message D · the benefits change explainer
artifacts.body: The medical plan changes at renewal. AI drafts the explainer from the plan documents; the benefits lead checks every figure, date and eligibility condition against the source and restores two exceptions the draft had dropped. It publishes under the People team's name, with a note that questions go to a named person. **Roughly 70% of the published words were AI-drafted.**

reasoning:
**C is the expensive one, and it's the smallest thing on the list.**

Start with what the message claims. A recognition note claims one thing: *I noticed you specifically.* That claim is the entire payload. There is no information in it, no deadline, no instruction. And the part carrying the claim is the specific: the detail only that director could have contributed, because she was there.

She gave the model a project title. **The model generated the specific**, which means the one element that made the message worth sending is the one element that was invented. Everything else (the warmth, the structure, the closing line) is exactly the median register the model produces for everyone.

Then it gets worse in a way unique to this format. Eight people received these in the same week. **Recognition notes get compared**: people screenshot them, forward them, mention them at lunch. The moment two of the eight sit next to each other, the identical structure is visible, and what the recipients learn isn't that AI was used. It is that the noticing didn't happen. You can't un-learn that about a manager.

And the perception gap makes it invisible from where the director sits. She read all eight and changed a word in two. From the inside, that's careful. She is rating her own AI use, which the research says she'll rate as fine at any level. The eight people are rating someone else's, at magnitude.

**A is the highest-volume AI use in the set and one of the cheapest.** Everything published descends from twenty-five minutes the COO actually spent thinking out loud. The position, the specifics and the stakes are all in the source; AI multiplied them. This is atomization working exactly as intended, on the highest-stakes subject on the list — which is the point. Sensitivity of topic isn't what determines cost.

**B is free.** A system notice claims no relationship. There is nothing to hollow out. Six minutes of human time on a logistics message is the correct amount, and the review against the ticket is what makes it safe.

**D is fine, and note why despite 70% AI-drafted words.** It publishes under the function's name rather than an individual's, so no one's personal credibility is staked on it; the payload is facts rather than relationship; and a human who could read the source restored two dropped exceptions, which is Module 5's omission catch, working. High AI proportion, low trust cost.
